name: Gloger's Rule
statement: Within a species, more heavily pigmented forms tend to live in more humid places.
meaning: Comparing populations of a single warm-blooded species across its range, individuals from warm, humid regions — often near the equator — tend to have darker fur, plumage, or skin, while those from drier regions tend to be paler. It is an ecogeographic correlation, not a law, and its cause is unsettled.
mechanism: Several explanations compete rather than combine. One is bacterial resistance: darker, eumelanin-rich feathers resist microbial breakdown better, favouring dark plumage where humid conditions carry higher bacterial loads. Others invoke camouflage against dark, dense humid habitats; a eumelanin-versus-pheomelanin split by climate; and UV protection or thermoregulation. The literature does not agree on a single dominant driver.

examples.text: The rule is well attested in birds: in one much-cited set, over ninety percent of a group of North American species conformed, with darker forms in humid areas and paler ones in arid regions.

Burtt and Ichida (2004) found that bacteria from humid-region song sparrows degraded feathers faster than those from arid-region birds, supporting a bacterial-resistance basis for darker plumage where it is wetter.

A latitude cline in human skin pigmentation is often cited as an extension, with acknowledged exceptions like Tibetans and the Inuit. This human application is contested, driven largely by UV rather than humidity, and socially sensitive — a related but not clean case.

variants.name: Bergmann's rule
variants.text: The body-size member of the ecogeographic trio: within a related group, colder-climate animals tend to be larger.

variants.name: Allen's rule
variants.text: The appendage member: colder-climate animals tend to have shorter limbs and extremities, reducing heat-losing surface.

variants.name: The bacterial-resistance hypothesis
variants.text: A specific mechanistic proposal for Gloger's rule — that melanin-rich plumage resists feather-degrading bacteria more common in humid climates — itself later questioned by other studies.

whyItMatters: It completes the classic trio of ecogeographic rules, adding coloration to size and shape as a trait that varies with climate. It is also a clean case of a solid pattern with an unsettled cause — the correlation is well documented, but which of several mechanisms drives it remains an open, actively debated question.

working.lead: Trust the pattern more than the cause
working.text: the humidity–pigmentation correlation in birds is well attested; the mechanism behind it is not, so describe the trend without committing to one explanation.
the rule compares populations of one species across its range, not unrelated species, and is grounded in endotherms.
the skin-colour cline is UV-driven rather than humidity-driven and is contested and sensitive, so it does not map cleanly onto the avian rule.

limits: The mechanism is genuinely unsettled — humidity and bacterial resistance, UV protection, camouflage, and thermoregulation are competing explanations with no consensus winner, and the bacterial-resistance claim itself has been challenged. Exceptions exist among species and populations. The human skin-colour extension is contested, driven by UV rather than humidity, and does not map cleanly onto the original avian rule. A 2019 review re-examined the rule's definitions and evidence, indicating its interpretation remains actively debated. The pattern is solid; the causal account is not.
misreadings: It is a correlation, not an explanation: the humidity–pigmentation link in birds is well documented, but its cause is disputed among several hypotheses. And it does not straightforwardly explain human skin colour, which tracks UV rather than humidity and is a contested, sensitive extension rather than a clean example.
origin: Named for the German-Silesian zoologist Constantin Wilhelm Lambert Gloger, who described the pattern in 1833 in a study of the covariation of climate and bird plumage colour; an earlier expression of the idea is sometimes credited to Peter Simon Pallas.

sources.text: Gloger's rule, Wikipedia. — the statement, the competing mechanisms, and the North American bird figure.
Burtt, E.H. & Ichida, J.M. (2004). "Gloger's Rule, Feather-Degrading Bacteria, and Color Variation Among Song Sparrows." The Condor, 106(3), 681–686.

Gunderson, A.R. et al. (2008). "Resistance of melanized feathers to bacterial degradation: is it really so black and white?" Journal of Avian Biology. — a challenge to the bacterial-resistance mechanism.
